teach.title: The word for the speaker
teach.say: Latin has its own small words for the one speaking and the one spoken to: **the personal pronouns (I, you, we, you all) and the reflexive sē ('-self')**. *ego* is I, *tū* is you (one person), *nōs* is we, *vōs* is you all. The verb ending already tells you who is acting, so *ego* and *tū* are put in only when the point is who, as against somebody else: *ego librum legō, tū dormīs* — I am reading, you are sleeping.

check.ask: Which word here names the person being spoken to?

teach.title: mē and mihi
teach.say: *ego* changes shape with the job it does. As the object it is *mē* — the accusative (the object form): *magister mē vocat*, the teacher calls me. When something comes to me it is *mihi* — the dative (the 'to/for' form): *pater mihi librum dat*, father gives me a book. *ego* itself is only ever the subject.

check.ask: Fill the two cells you have just met: me as object, and to/for me.

teach.title: tē and tibi
teach.say: *tū* works exactly like *ego*: the object is *tē*, the 'to/for you' form is *tibi*. Hear the rhyme and you have both tables: *mē / tē*, *mihi / tibi*. In *magister tibi virgam ostendit*, *tibi* is the one shown to and *virgam* the thing shown.

check.ask: Fill the two cells for tū: you as object, and to/for you.

teach.title: The plurals nōs and vōs
teach.say: For more than one Latin has *nōs* (we, us) and *vōs* (you all). Each is the same word as subject and as object — *nōs in hortō sumus*, we are in the garden; *magister nōs vocat*, the teacher calls us — so only the sentence tells you which job it is doing. For 'to or for' them Latin says *nōbīs* and *vōbīs*.

check.ask: Iūlius ____ pecūniam dat, vōbīs nihil. Which word means 'to us'?

teach.title: sē points back to the subject
teach.say: *sē* means the subject itself — himself, herself, itself, themselves — and it has no nominative (the subject form), because it can never be the subject: *Iūlia sē in speculō videt*, Julia sees herself. Its 'to or for' form is *sibi*, to or for himself. When the other person is somebody else, Latin uses a demonstrative used as a pronoun (is = he, ea = she, id = it): *Quīntus eum nōn amat* is about another person, not about Quintus.

check.ask: Which word here means Marcus himself, rather than another person?

teach.title: mēcum, tēcum, sēcum
teach.say: With *cum* (with) these pronouns turn round and glue the preposition on the back: *mēcum* with me, *tēcum* with you, *sēcum* with himself, *nōbīscum* with us, *vōbīscum* with you all. Latin never writes *cum mē*. *Mārcus sēcum librum portat* — Marcus carries a book with him. One row of these tables is left for later: the genitive (the 'of' form) — *meī, tuī, nostrum, vestrum, suī* — is rare, and the book comes back to it when it is needed.

check.ask: Venī ____ in hortum, Iūlia! Which one word means 'with me'?

core.text: *I, you, we, you all* have their own small tables: **the personal pronouns (I, you, we, you all) and the reflexive se ('-self')**. *ego* (I): *mē, meī, mihi, mē*; *tū* (you): *tē, tuī, tibi, tē*; *nōs* (we): *nōs, nostrum, nōbīs, nōbīs*; *vōs* (you all): *vōs, vestrum, vōbīs, vōbīs*. *sē* (himself, herself, themselves) points back to the subject and has no nominative: *sē, suī, sibi, sē*. Latin name: prōnōmina persōnālia et reflexīvum.
*I / me* is the same idea: the form changes with the job — *I* is the subject form, *me* the object form. A reflexive points back to the subject: *he sees himself*.
Subject ego / tū / nōs / vōs appears only for emphasis; sē means the subject itself, never someone else.

*He, she, it* are not personal pronouns in Latin; they are *is, ea, id*, a demonstrative used as a pronoun (is = he, ea = she, id = it). *eum* is someone else, *sē* the subject itself: Quintus says *sē aegrum esse* — that he himself is ill; *eum aegrum esse* — that another person is.

more.text: With *cum* (with) the pronouns glue together: *mēcum, tēcum, sēcum, nōbīscum* — with me, with you, with himself, with us. The genitives *meī, tuī, suī, nostrum, vestrum* never mean *my, your*; they do other genitive jobs — as a partitive (*nēmō nostrum* — none of us) or with words like *memor* (mindful of). *Nostrī / vestrī* go with feelings: *amor nostrī* — love of us. For *my, your, his own* Latin uses the adjectives *meus, tuus, suus*; *suus* is reflexive like *sē*: *Iūlius fīlium suum vocat* — his own son; for someone else's son, *fīlium eius*.

The learner's notes (week 15): first person includes the speaker, second the audience, third neither; Latin has *ego / nōs* and *tū / vōs*, and any demonstrative serves as a third-person pronoun. The five-case tables are *ego, mē, meī, mihi, mē*; *tū, tē, tuī, tibi, tē*; *nōs, nōs, nostrum, nōbīs, nōbīs*; *vōs, vōs, vestrum, vōbīs, vōbīs*. The reflexive exists only in the third person, with one set of forms for singular and plural and no nominative (*sē, suī, sibi, sē*); the four pronouns look alike case by case (*mē / tē / sē*, *mihi / tibi / sibi*); possession uses *meus, tuus, suus, noster, vester*.

Ørberg (chapter XV): *nōs* and *vōs* are the same in the nominative and the accusative; *ego nōn rīdeō, quia vōs mē rīdētis*. A&G add the emphatic forms *egomet* (I myself), *tūte*, and *sēsē* for *sē*.
